title: Understanding Big-O Notation
summary: Big-O describes how an algorithm's work (time complexity) and extra memory (space complexity) grow as the input grows. The lesson walks through O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²), O(2ⁿ) and O(n!) and shows how to spot each one from code patterns like loops, nested loops, halving and recursion. Step-by-step guide arrives when the lecture is published.
goal: Look at a short function and state its time and space complexity with a one-line reason.

steps.title: Read the lesson and its cheat sheet
steps.detail: Read the Big-O page through the 'Quick Identification Cheat Sheet'. Notice that time and space are judged separately.
steps.doneWhen: You can name the code pattern behind each of the seven complexities.

steps.title: Feel the difference between O(n) and O(log n)
steps.detail: Run this in python3. It uses the curriculum's linear and binary search and counts loop steps on a million sorted numbers.
steps.doneWhen: Linear search takes about 1,000,000 steps; binary search takes about 20.

steps.title: Label four functions before peeking
steps.detail: Cover the answers and label double_values, print_pairs, create_pairs and fibonacci from the lesson with time and space Big-O. Then check yourself against the page.
steps.doneWhen: You got at least 6 of the 8 labels (4 time, 4 space) right.

steps.title: Practice saying it like an interview
steps.detail: In a technical interview you talk through the approach and its Big-O before coding. For each function above, say out loud: 'Time is O(...) because..., space is O(...) because...'. Skim the curriculum's Technical Interviews page for the full process.
steps.doneWhen: You can explain each answer out loud in under 30 seconds.

concepts.meaning: A way to describe how work or memory grows as the input gets bigger.
How the number of steps grows with input size.
How much extra memory the algorithm creates as input grows (not counting the input).
The problem is cut in half each step, so it grows very slowly, like binary search.
Memory used by recursive calls waiting to finish; it counts toward space complexity.
